schema.description: {{COMPANY_NAME}} reusable Merlino Catalogue threat-profile template for System Integrator / MSP organisations. TP-10 models Third-Party / Supplier Compromise in both directions: Supplier→Organisation and Organisation→Customer. It covers trusted relationships, vendor/MSP identities, VPN and remote support, RMM, delegated/cloud accounts, OAuth/PAT/service-token integrations, software/dependency/build/update supply chains, hardware supply chain, code repositories, cross-boundary discovery/lateral movement, SaaS/data access, exfiltration and ransomware/destructive follow-on. The profile incorporates MITRE T1199/T1195, current DET0488 third-party detection guidance, M-Trends 2026 SaaS-vendor/PAT findings and CISA MSP/RMM guidance while remaining reusable and actor-neutral. Organisation is represented by {{COMPANY_NAME}}.

data.Name: TP-10 | Gather Victim Org Information: Business Relationships
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Identify customers, suppliers, MSPs, SaaS vendors, cloud partners, resellers, managed-service providers and technology dependencies that possess trusted access or sensitive information. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Third-party compromise is impossible to model without understanding who trusts whom. System integrators sit in dense trust graphs and may both consume privileged supplier services and hold privileged access into downstream customers. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Trust Mapping. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Supplier relationships, Customer relationships, MSP contracts, SaaS integrations, Cloud partner relationships. Detection opportunities: Third-party inventory review; Attack-surface correlation; Unexpected vendor/customer identity activity. Defensive considerations: Maintain authoritative third-party trust inventory; Classify access type and privilege; Review trust at onboarding/offboarding.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Third-party compromise is impossible to model without understanding who trusts whom. System integrators sit in dense trust graphs and may both consume privileged supplier services and hold privileged access into downstream customers. Threat-led context: ATT&CK T1199 explicitly models abuse of organisations that already have access to intended victims. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Core; Phase=Trust Mapping; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. It covers supplier/MSP/customer identities, vendor VPN and remote support, RMM, SaaS/OAuth/PAT integrations, delegated cloud access, software/dependency/hardware supply chains, code repositories and service connections, cross-boundary lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and destructive/ransomware follow-on. Both inbound Supplier→Organisation and outbound Organisation→Customer paths are included because a system integrator may be victim and stepping stone simultaneously. TP-02/TP-03 provide deeper Microsoft partner/customer pivot coverage; TP-05 deeper CI/CD supply-chain detail; TP-09 deeper SaaS data theft. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-10 | Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Identify staff and external contacts responsible for vendor management, support, managed services, remote access, SaaS administration and customer administration. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Role discovery helps attackers target identities that can approve support access, reset credentials, authorize integrations or move between organisations. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Trust Mapping. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Vendor managers, Support engineers, Customer admins, MSP operators, SaaS admins. Detection opportunities: Targeting intelligence; Role-based phishing patterns. Defensive considerations: Separate privileged identities; Strong vendor verification; Least privilege.

data.Name: TP-10 | Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Obtain credentials belonging to supplier administrators, MSP operators, customer support accounts, external consultants or integration identities. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Credentials associated with third parties often have legitimate remote or SaaS access and may receive less scrutiny than internal administrator accounts. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Targeting. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Vendor accounts, Customer support accounts, MSP identities, Guest/B2B users, Service accounts. Detection opportunities: Leaked credential monitoring; Third-party risky-signin correlation. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named accounts; Rapid credential revocation; No shared vendor accounts.

data.Name: TP-10 | Phishing: Spearphishing via Service
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Use Teams, messaging or other external services to phish partner/customer personnel. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Third-party staff often collaborate across tenants and may treat cross-company service messages as normal. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Third-Party Initial Access. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Teams, SaaS messaging, Support channels. Detection opportunities: External collaboration anomalies. Defensive considerations: Cross-tenant controls; Verified support channels.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Third-party staff often collaborate across tenants and may treat cross-company service messages as normal. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to third-party, supplier, MSP, SaaS integration or customer trust compromise. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Core; Phase=Third-Party Initial Access; Priority=High; Confidence=High. data.Name: TP-10 | Remote Access Tools: Remote Desktop Software
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Use legitimate remote monitoring and management or remote desktop software to access downstream systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: RMM tools are a uniquely important third-party risk because one management platform can reach many endpoints or customers and is often trusted/allow-listed. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: MSP / Support Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Trusted Remote Administration. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: RMM console, Remote support agents, Managed endpoints, Customer servers. Detection opportunities: Unexpected RMM operator/source; Mass sessions; Access outside ticket/change window. Defensive considerations: MFA; Named operators; Session recording; Approval/ticket correlation; Restrict unattended access.

data.Description: Steal OAuth, personal access, application or API tokens associated with a supplier SaaS integration or trusted application. data.Name: TP-10 | Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Replay a stolen third-party session to operate inside the trusted application or customer environment. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Session replay preserves the identity and trust context of the original external user. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Cloud / SaaS. Third-party lifecycle phase: Replay Trusted Third-Party Session. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: SaaS, Partner portal, Customer portal. Detection opportunities: New IP/device for same session. Defensive considerations: Rapid revocation; Session binding.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Session replay preserves the identity and trust context of the original external user. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to third-party, supplier, MSP, SaaS integration or customer trust compromise. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Cloud / SaaS; Phase=Replay Trusted Third-Party Session; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. Defensive considerations: App allow-list; Admin consent workflow; Per-customer least privilege; Periodic review.

data.Name: TP-10 | Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Grant additional roles to supplier/customer identities or integration principals. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Excessive external privilege increases both immediate blast radius and downstream trust abuse. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Cloud. Third-party lifecycle phase: Expand Third-Party Cloud Privilege. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Entra roles, Azure RBAC, SaaS admin roles. Detection opportunities: New role assigned to guest/vendor/app. Defensive considerations: PIM; Approval; Guest/external role alerts.

Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Attacker-created external-looking or support accounts can outlive remediation of the original compromise. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Privileged Cloud. Third-party lifecycle phase: Create New Trusted Cloud Account. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Cloud tenant, SaaS accounts. Detection opportunities: Account creation outside lifecycle process; New external user plus privilege. Defensive considerations: Lifecycle governance; Approval; Access reviews.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Attacker-created external-looking or support accounts can outlive remediation of the original compromise. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to third-party, supplier, MSP, SaaS integration or customer trust compromise. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Privileged Cloud; Phase=Create New Trusted Cloud Account; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. It covers supplier/MSP/customer identities, vendor VPN and remote support, RMM, SaaS/OAuth/PAT integrations, delegated cloud access, software/dependency/hardware supply chains, code repositories and service connections, cross-boundary lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and destructive/ransomware follow-on. Both inbound Supplier→Organisation and outbound Organisation→Customer paths are included because a system integrator may be victim and stepping stone simultaneously. TP-02/TP-03 provide deeper Microsoft partner/customer pivot coverage; TP-05 deeper CI/CD supply-chain detail; TP-09 deeper SaaS data theft. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-10 | Modify Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Add attacker-controlled MFA or weaken authentication for a trusted external identity. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: This converts a transient external-account takeover into durable access. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Identity. Third-party lifecycle phase: Modify MFA on Third-Party Account. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: MFA methods, Supplier/customer identities. Detection opportunities: MFA method changes on external account. Defensive considerations: Strong identity proofing; Alert on third-party MFA changes.

data.Name: TP-10 | Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Modify access policies or exclusions so vendor/customer identities bypass strong requirements. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A compromised admin may deliberately carve out an external identity from protective controls. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Privileged Cloud. Third-party lifecycle phase: Weaken Policy for External / Vendor Access. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Conditional Access, Trusted locations, External users. Detection opportunities: New external-user exclusion; Policy change after partner compromise. Defensive considerations: PIM; Protected policy admins; Alert on exclusions.

data.Name: TP-10 | Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Manipulate third-party libraries, packages, CI/CD actions, IDE extensions, development tools or dependencies before they are consumed. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: A system integrator depends on large third-party software ecosystems and also creates software consumed by customers. A compromised dependency can therefore impact both directions of the trust chain. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Software Supply Chain. Third-party lifecycle phase: Software Supply Chain. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Open-source packages, CI/CD actions, IDE extensions, Build tools, Package registries. Detection opportunities: Dependency/provenance changes; New package maintainer; Unexpected install-time egress. Defensive considerations: Pin dependencies; SBOM; Provenance/signatures; Private mirrors; Dependency review.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. data.Name: TP-10 | Software Deployment Tools
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Use software deployment, RMM, package deployment or update tooling to distribute attacker-controlled software to trusted systems. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Deployment platforms multiply blast radius because one management channel can install software across many internal or customer endpoints. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core MSP / Software Delivery. Third-party lifecycle phase: Abuse Trusted Software Deployment Mechanism. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Software deployment, RMM, Package distribution, Update services. Detection opportunities: Mass deployment outside change window; New package/publisher; Unsigned/unexpected payload. Defensive considerations: Separation of duties; Code signing; Approval; Change correlation.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Deployment platforms multiply blast radius because one management channel can install software across many internal or customer endpoints. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to third-party, supplier, MSP, SaaS integration or customer trust compromise. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Core MSP / Software Delivery; Phase=Abuse Trusted Software Deployment Mechanism; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. It covers supplier/MSP/customer identities, vendor VPN and remote support, RMM, SaaS/OAuth/PAT integrations, delegated cloud access, software/dependency/hardware supply chains, code repositories and service connections, cross-boundary lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and destructive/ransomware follow-on. Both inbound Supplier→Organisation and outbound Organisation→Customer paths are included because a system integrator may be victim and stepping stone simultaneously. TP-02/TP-03 provide deeper Microsoft partner/customer pivot coverage; TP-05 deeper CI/CD supply-chain detail; TP-09 deeper SaaS data theft. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.

data.Name: TP-10 | Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Search supplier or integrator files, scripts, documentation and deployment artifacts for credentials and keys that enable trusted access. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Third-party environments frequently contain connection instructions, customer credentials, support passwords and service tokens. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Harvest Vendor / Customer Credentials from Files. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Scripts, Configs, Support docs, Deployment files. Detection opportunities: Secret-pattern access/search; Bulk config reads. Defensive considerations: Central secret management; No plaintext credentials; Secret scanning.

Threat-led context: C r e d e n t i a l   E x p a n s i o n Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Core; Phase=Harvest Vendor / Customer Credentials from Files; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. data.Name: TP-10 | Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Use third-party credentials to access Windows systems over RDP. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: RDP is common in support arrangements and may provide direct privileged customer/server access. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Windows / Managed Service. Third-party lifecycle phase: Move via RDP from Vendor / MSP Access. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Windows servers, Jump hosts, Customer systems. Detection opportunities: RDP by vendor identity outside ticket/window. Defensive considerations: MFA; Gateway; Session recording; Segmentation.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: RDP is common in support arrangements and may provide direct privileged customer/server access. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to third-party, supplier, MSP, SaaS integration or customer trust compromise. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Windows / Managed Service; Phase=Move via RDP from Vendor / MSP Access; Priority=Critical; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. data.Description: Use WMI for remote execution after trusted Windows access is obtained. Defensive considerations: Restrict WMI; EDR.

data.Description: Use legitimate web services for C2, staging or coordination. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Trusted web services may be broadly reachable from management networks. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Core. Third-party lifecycle phase: Use Trusted Web Services from Supplier / Customer Environment. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Cloud/web services. Detection opportunities: Rare service use from management host. Defensive considerations: SaaS governance; Egress controls.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Trusted web services may be broadly reachable from management networks. data.Name: TP-10 | Data Destruction
data.Source: X3M.AI Threat Profile - System Integrator - TP-10 Third-Party / Supplier Compromise
data.Description: Delete data or resources accessible through supplier/customer trust. Why it matters for a system integrator/MSP: Trusted administrative access can enable destruction even without ransomware. Direction: Bidirectional. Applicability: Destructive Follow-on. Third-party lifecycle phase: Destroy Data Through Trusted Access. Primary assets/trust channels at risk: Customer data, Cloud resources, Supplier systems. Detection opportunities: Mass delete by external/vendor identity. Defensive considerations: Retention/versioning; Resource locks; Backups.
data.Notes: Threat Profile TP-10 | Generic System Integrator / MSP Third-Party / Supplier Compromise profile | Organisation placeholder: {{COMPANY_NAME}}. Inclusion rationale: Trusted administrative access can enable destruction even without ransomware. Threat-led context: Technique included because it is structurally relevant to third-party, supplier, MSP, SaaS integration or customer trust compromise. Direction=Bidirectional; Applicability=Destructive Follow-on; Phase=Destroy Data Through Trusted Access; Priority=High; Confidence=High. Scope boundary: TP-10 models compromise through organisational trust relationships rather than one specific technology. It covers supplier/MSP/customer identities, vendor VPN and remote support, RMM, SaaS/OAuth/PAT integrations, delegated cloud access, software/dependency/hardware supply chains, code repositories and service connections, cross-boundary lateral movement, data collection/exfiltration and destructive/ransomware follow-on. Both inbound Supplier→Organisation and outbound Organisation→Customer paths are included because a system integrator may be victim and stepping stone simultaneously. TP-02/TP-03 provide deeper Microsoft partner/customer pivot coverage; TP-05 deeper CI/CD supply-chain detail; TP-09 deeper SaaS data theft. This record is threat-profile intelligence, not evidence of activity in a specific organisation.
